title: Box by box: one patient, three algorithms
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Mrs. Remedios Aquino, 72, on a beta-blocker, is two hours into dialysis in Iloilo City. She is drowsy but opens her eyes to her name. You are the physician-on-duty, just arrived with the defibrillator.

n1.prompt: Which algorithm is she in, and what is your first move?

choices.text: Bradycardia with a pulse, unstable (low pressure, drowsy): monitor and pads on, oxygen, IV access, atropine per protocol, and look for causes (potassium, the beta-blocker).
choices.feedback: Five questions: responsive (barely), breathing, definite pulse, not an arrest rhythm, unstable. That places her in unstable bradycardia.
She has a pulse and responds. Compressions are for absent circulation.
choices.then: A nurse feels a pulse and stops you. You treat unstable bradycardia.

choices.text: Intradialytic hypotension: saline bolus and observe.
choices.feedback: A heart rate of 38 with drowsiness is a rhythm problem first; fluid alone misses the cause.
choices.then: You see the rate and treat unstable bradycardia.

n2.scene: While pads go on and atropine is drawn up, she stops answering. Slow gasps. No definite carotid pulse in 10 seconds.

choices.text: “No pulse. Cardiac arrest. Compressions now, chair flat.” Stop the pacing plan; the recorder notes the time.
choices.feedback: Announcing the transition closes the old plan for everyone at once.

choices.text: “Increase the pacer current and give another atropine.”
choices.feedback: Pacing and atropine belong to bradycardia with a pulse. Without a pulse, only compressions move blood.
choices.then: Thirty seconds later the recorder says no one has checked a pulse. You call the arrest.

choices.text: Wait for the atropine to work before deciding.
choices.feedback: Gasping without a pulse is cardiac arrest now; waiting withholds compressions.

n3.scene: Compressions are running. The monitor shows organized slow wide complexes.
n3.prompt: Which arrest path, and which cause do you raise first?

choices.text: Nonshockable (PEA): epinephrine as soon as feasible, two-minute cycles, and treat potassium and the beta-blocker as likely causes (BRASH), per protocol.
choices.feedback: Organized electricity without a pulse is PEA. In a dialysis patient on a beta-blocker, potassium and the drug together top the cause list.
PEA is not shockable; a shock wastes time and pauses compressions.
choices.then: The leader corrects the path to nonshockable.

choices.text: Nonshockable path, but look for causes later once the physician has time.
choices.feedback: The path is right, but in PEA finding the cause is the treatment; ask now.
choices.then: You raise potassium at the next cycle.

n4.scene: After epinephrine and potassium treatment per protocol, the rhythm check shows a narrow rhythm at 72. A nurse feels a strong carotid pulse; pressure 96/60.

choices.text: Post-ROSC care: keep pads on, oxygen titrated, MAP target, 12-lead ECG, glucose and potassium, call the attending nephrologist and the transfer.
choices.feedback: A definite pulse and pressure is ROSC: the third algorithm in ten minutes. Pads stay on because re-arrest is common.

choices.text: Keep compressing until the ambulance arrives.
choices.feedback: Compressing over a strong pulse is unnecessary; reassessment exists to catch this change.
choices.then: The recorder points out the pulse; compressions stop.

end.text: Mrs. Aquino is transferred with a pulse after passing through three algorithms: unstable bradycardia, PEA arrest, and post-ROSC care. Each transition was announced aloud.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Five questions place the patient; ask them again at every reassessment.
  • Announce transitions aloud. “No pulse, cardiac arrest” closes the previous plan.
  • Slow rhythm plus a rate-slowing drug in a dialysis patient means potassium and BRASH until proven otherwise.
